title: The Camino de Santiago
hookLine: walkers from everywhere follow yellow arrows to Compostela

lines: A SCALLOP SHELL ON A BACKPACK.
cards: A yellow arrow, painted on the corner of a stone wall in a Spanish village. Another on a lamppost. Another on a rock beside a dirt track through wheat fields.
Follow them long enough and they lead to a cathedral. A woman with a scallop shell tied to her backpack passes a farmer leaning on a gate. He nods and says two words.
Buen camino. Good road. Further on, a teenager with blistered feet hears it from a café owner, then from a limping pilgrim twice his age.
Said that often, the words start to feel like a blessing.

teach.b: The Camino de Santiago is the Way of Saint James: a web of pilgrim routes across Spain, Portugal and France, all ending at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, in Spain's northwest corner.
You met James on his feast day, back in year three. Santiago is Spanish for Saint James, the apostle, son of Zebedee and brother of John.

teach.h: KILLED WITH THE SWORD, ACTS SAYS.
teach.b: Acts records his death in a single line, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword." That's Herod. Scripture says no more.

Tradition says much more: that James had preached in Spain, that his body was carried there, and that his tomb lies beneath the cathedral. The Church honors the tradition; historians debate it. Both can be said honestly.

teach.h: A SHELL, A STAMP, A CERTIFICATE.
teach.b: The scallop shell became the pilgrim's badge. Walkers carry a credential, a little folded booklet stamped at churches, hostels and cafés along the way.
Arriving with it, a pilgrim can ask the cathedral office for a certificate called the Compostela. Then, the people.
Some walk out of devotion, some out of grief, some to keep a vow, some after a hard year, some out of curiosity. The arrows don't ask why. Last, the greeting.
It's a wish shared between strangers going the same way.
But it carries what Emmaus showed yesterday: the stranger who falls into step beside you may be going the same way home.

how: Pilgrims walk, cycle or ride sections of the Camino to the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, carrying a credential stamped along the way, attending pilgrim Masses and greeting one another with "buen camino."

games.q: what does “the camino de santiago” mean?
o: the Way of Saint James, routes to his shrine
a Spanish feast day for the apostle James
the road two friends walked to Emmaus

p: a booklet stamped along the way
good road, a wish between walkers

s: the Bible says Saint James is buried in Spain
Acts records only his death by the sword in Jerusalem. the tomb at Compostela is held by tradition.
Camino pilgrims carry a credential that gets stamped
a folded booklet, stamped at churches, hostels and cafés along the route.
buen camino is a formal prayer of the Church
it's a greeting between walkers: good road.

games.q: you've walked into Santiago de Compostela with a full credential of stamps. what can you ask for at the cathedral's pilgrim office?
games.why: the Compostela, a certificate for pilgrims who arrive with their stamped credential.

practice: Think of a walk you already take: to the car, to the mailbox, around the block with the dog. Picture going one corner past where you usually turn back, and who you might pass there; a nod is enough.
If you pray, offer those extra steps for someone on a hard road of their own; if you don't, just walk them on purpose.

wordCard.voice: The Camino de Santiago. The Way of Saint James: pilgrim routes that end at his shrine in Compostela, marked by yellow arrows and scallop shells. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: James, the apostle's name as the New Testament writes it. Santiago is how Spanish says Saint James.

carryVoice: Your line: buen camino. Two words, said between strangers going the same way. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.q: And he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.
